lines.text: What if you could lock in today's price, and decide later if you even want to buy? That's an option.
A call option is the right, but not the duty, to buy a stock at a fixed price, called the strike, before a set date.
That right costs a small fee, the premium. Say the stock is a hundred. You pay three dollars for the right to buy it at a hundred.
If the stock jumps to a hundred and twenty, your right is worth about twenty. Your three dollars became twenty!
If it falls, you just walk away. The most you can lose is the three dollars you paid.
A put is the mirror: the right to sell at the strike. It pays off when the stock falls, like insurance on your shares.
But options melt. Every day, part of the premium disappears. That's time decay.
And it speeds up at the end. In the last weeks, the melting gets fast, like an ice cube in the sun.
Who gets that melting money? The option seller. They collect premium every day, and hope nothing big happens.
One more thing: when traders expect big moves, options get more expensive. That's volatility.
So why do people love options? Small cost, a capped loss for buyers, huge upside, and a way to insure what you own.
Not financial advice. Time is working against every option you buy, so know your date.
Send this to a friend on Orbi Transfer. Now you know!
